scenes.tts: Tap the tendon below your kneecap, and your leg kicks. The path through the spinal cord has only one synapse between the sensor and the motor neuron. Why only one? And what does that same stretch do to the muscle on the other side of the joint?

scenes.tts: The sensor is a muscle spindle. It lies parallel to the ordinary fibres that make force. A tendon tap gives a brief stretch, and that stretches the spindle. Its one A afferents respond to the speed and the amount of stretch. They fire. They enter the cord through the dorsal root, and they branch.

Its Ia afferents respond to the speed and the amount of stretch. They fire. They enter the cord through the dorsal root, and they branch.
scenes.visual: Question marks resolve into a spindle beside the ordinary fibres; the afferent carries spikes into the dorsal side of the cord and splits at a branch point.
scenes.narration: The sensor is a muscle spindle. It lies parallel to the ordinary fibres that make force. A tendon tap gives a brief stretch, and that stretches the spindle. scenes.tts: One branch excites the motor neurons of the same muscle, directly. That is one synapse, so the path is monosynaptic. These are alpha motor neurons. Their cell bodies sit in the ventral horn, and their axons leave through the ventral root. The muscle contracts against the stretch. Only this branch is monosynaptic. The reflex as a whole is not.

scenes.visual: A spike runs down branch one to the motor neuron across one green synapse; the muscle shortens and turns green.

scenes.tts: The other branch excites an inhibitory interneuron, on the same side of the cord. That interneuron inhibits the motor neurons of the antagonist, the muscle that moves the joint the other way. This path has two synapses, so it is disynaptic. It stays on the same side.

scenes.visual: A spike runs along branch two to a red interneuron (synapse one) and from it to the antagonist's motor neuron (synapse two, red bar end); the other half of the cord stays empty.

scenes.tts: In decerebrate cats, Sherrington found that when a reflex excites one muscle, the muscle that opposes it at the same joint relaxes. He called the pairing reciprocal innervation. The crossed-extensor reflex is the one that crosses. A painful stimulus to one foot makes that leg withdraw, and the other leg takes the weight. It is polysynaptic and bilateral. The stretch reflex is local and one-sided.

scenes.visual: Both paths fire together, the antagonist relaxes; then a grey dashed arrow crosses the midline for the crossed-extensor reflex while the stretch circuit stays on one side.

scenes.tts: So one stretch sends two commands. One synapse excites the motor neurons of the same muscle. Two synapses, through an interneuron on the same side, inhibit the antagonist. The rule to keep: a stretch excites the same muscle and inhibits its antagonist, on the same side.
